Case Study Template (Rough Draft)

2026-07-28

Overview and Recommended AGWRC

AGWRC analysis for USGS 01672500: SOUTH ANNA RIVER NEAR ASHLAND, VA. The regression should not be used for predictions. This gage has a very weak, positive regression fit, and the regression performed very poorly during historical events (consistently underpredicted). While the BPJ method was used for almost all the case study events, there was not a constant BPJ that performed well consistently; values ranged from 0.9667 to 0.988 depending on the start date and the initial flow.

Terminology

Regression AGWRC: the AGWRC calculated by imputing starting flow from manually selected flow event into AGWRC vs Flow Regression

Event AGWRC: the AGWRC from a known baseflow event identified by the workflow

Iterative AGWRC: the manually selected AGWRC that provides the “best fit” for the manually selected baseflow event

Starting flow: the observed flow at the first day of the manually selected baseflow event

MAE: Mean Absolute Error

RMSE: Root Mean Square Error

MAPE: Mean Absolute Percentage Error

Regression Analysis

Image 1. AGWRC vs Flow Regression

AGWRC vs Median Flow Regression. 44 baseflow events were identified at USGS 01638500. An AGWRC value was calculated for each event based on the exponential decay of flow during the identified baseflow event. The R-squared value is: 0.042545. Little of the observed variation in the data can be explained by the regression model. Historically, the regression has not consistenty performed well at other gages with similar R-squared values.

QC Metrics

There are 44 identified baseflow events at this gage. As discussed further in the DA Analysis Summary in Appendix A, the number of identified baseflow events is dependent on the record length of the gage; older gages have more identified baseflow events. Additionally, ten baseflow events has been deemed the appropriate number of baseflow events to perform reasonable analysis.

Table ?. Other relevant QC metrics. The Breusch–Pagan test and the White test are statistical methods to quantify heteroscedasticity (when the variability of the dependent variable is not constant). Both tests check for heteroskedasticity; the Breusch–Pagan test assumes normal residuals and detects linear heteroscedasticity while the White test is more general and detects both linear and nonlinear heteroskedasticity. A significant p-value (less than 0.05) suggests sufficient evidence for heteroskedasticity in the flow data. The recorded flow values indicate the gage length, or the total number of non-NA flow values recorded over the entire date range of data collection. The watershed slope is the average slope in the entire drainage basin expressed as a percentage of the vertical rise over the the horizontal distance.
